nameStory: The cup-and-saucer vine gets its charming name from its distinctive flowers, which look remarkably like an elegant teacup sitting on a delicate saucer. The bell-shaped flower forms the 'cup' while the large, flat green sepals beneath create the perfect 'saucer' - nature's own tea service! It's also called cathedral bells or monastery bells because the drooping flowers resemble the bells that call worshippers to prayer.
description: Cup-and-saucer vine is a vigorous climbing vine native to Mexico that's occasionally grown as an ornamental in New England gardens. This fast-growing annual can reach 15-25 feet in a single season, using tendrils to scramble up fences, trellises, or other supports. The most striking feature is its large, bell-shaped flowers that dangle downward like purple or white church bells, each sitting on a prominent green 'saucer' of sepals. With only one recorded sighting in New England, this is truly a rare garden escape to treasure if you spot it.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large bell-shaped flowers, 2-3 inches long, that hang downward like church bells. They start greenish-white and age to deep purple or violet, with a sweet, honey-like fragrance most noticeable in the evening. Each flower sits on a prominent flat green 'saucer' of sepals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 4-6 oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem. The end leaflet is often replaced by a curly tendril that feels slightly sticky and helps the vine climb. Leaves have a soft, slightly fuzzy texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Vigorous climbing vine that can grow 15-25 feet in one season. Uses branching tendrils to grip and climb any available support, creating dense coverage. Stems are green and somewhat succulent when young.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large egg-shaped seed capsules that split open to reveal flat, papery seeds with distinctive wing-like edges. Capsules start green and turn brown when mature, making a dry rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: In New England, this is almost exclusively found as a garden escape near homes, parks, or botanical gardens where it was cultivated as an ornamental vine. It prefers rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, often scrambling over fences, arbors, or garden structures. Given its tropical origins, it cannot survive New England winters and appears only as an annual escape.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from seed in late spring, initially forming low rosettes of compound leaves before beginning their climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with the spectacular cup-and-saucer flowers appearing continuously. Vines reach maximum size and coverage during hot summer months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the formation of distinctive egg-shaped seed capsules. Plants begin to decline with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies completely with hard frost, leaving only dried stems and empty seed capsules. Seeds may overwinter to germinate the following spring.

funFact: This vine is a master of timing - its flowers open in the late afternoon and evening, releasing their sweet fragrance to attract night-flying pollinators like hawk moths, then the fragrance fades by morning as day-shift pollinators take over!
confusionNotes: The large bell-shaped flowers sitting on flat green sepals make this vine nearly unmistakable - no other climbing plant in New England has this distinctive cup-and-saucer flower structure. Morning glories have similar climbing habit but trumpet-shaped flowers without the prominent green 'saucer' underneath.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Mexican ivy,' this plant is not related to true ivy at all - it belongs to the phlox family. The name likely comes from its vigorous climbing habit and Mexican origin, but unlike true ivy, it's an annual that dies with frost and has completely different flowers and leaves.
compareHints: Cup-and-saucer vine is the only member of the Cobaea genus found in New England. Among other members of the phlox family, it's unique for being a climbing vine - most other phlox family members are upright herbs or small shrubs with very different flower structures. The closest relatives in our region would be garden phlox or wild phlox, but these have flat, five-petaled flowers in clusters rather than large hanging bells.
